documents: Hirschberg & Sutherland (2022), A Kinematic Model of Quaternary Fault Slip Rates and Distributed Deformation at the New Zealand Plate Boundary, JGR Solid Earth 127, e2022JB024828 (published PDF, 22 pages)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (printed as 'N of 22', identical to PDF pages counted from 1)

entry.evidence: making constructions of kinematic models into non-trivial tasks.

steps.action: Pose the aim: a kinematic model of New Zealand that fits fault slip-rate and off-fault deformation observations under known plate-motion constraints, unlike continuum or rigid-block models.
steps.quote: We present a kinematic model of New Zealand that fits observations of deformation within the plate-boundary zone

steps.action: Adopt the faulted thin-sheet regression method and codes of Haines and Sutherland (2018), co-authored by the second author.
steps.quote: We adopt the thin-sheet solution method of Haines and Sutherland (2018), which accounts for discontinuities at faults

steps.action: Take Quaternary geological fault slip rates, rakes and dips from the Litchfield et al. (2014) active fault model, convert them to horizontal rates, and fold small faults into strain-rate observations by Kostrov summation.
steps.quote: We use slip rates given by Litchfield et al. (2014) as our primary set of

steps.action: Design the model domain: MORVEL plate velocities as exact eastern and western boundary conditions, interpolated northern and southern boundaries (Havre Trough opening 20 mm/yr, Puysegur Ridge 14 mm/yr), rigid regions from seismic-reflection mapping, and a triangular mesh with faults as velocity discontinuities.
steps.quote: We use velocities specified by MORVEL (DeMets et al., 2010).

steps.action: Revise auxiliary observation uncertainties: inflate them on the Hikurangi and Puysegur thrusts and on poorly known offshore faults (factor five), assign nominal rates and rakes to unrated faults, and use the long-term Akatore Fault rate.
steps.quote: To reflect this, we use the slip-rate estimates of Litchfield et al. (2014) but with larger uncertainties

steps.action: Construct synthetic strain-rate style (A0) and maximum-shortening-direction observations by smoothing on-fault slip with a 25 km taper, so that off-fault deformation keeps the style of nearby faults.
steps.quote: We construct a set of synthetic off-fault deformation-style observations (with uncertainties) by regional smoothing of on-fault observations

steps.action: Iterate an a priori viscous thin-sheet solution and an a posteriori weighted least-squares regression, adjusting force potentials and then slip-rate capacities until the fit stabilizes, with Monte Carlo resampling of slip-rate observations for uncertainties.
steps.quote: we then infer a kinematic solution (our primary objective) that departs from physical principles to fit observations

steps.action: Vary the uniform strain-rate capacity eta from 1e-11 to 1e-4 per year, record the residual sum of squares to fault observations, and select the best-fitting model HS22-Lit (eta = 2e-6 per year).
steps.quote: and optimize to find the a posteriori quality of fit to observations of fault slip rate

steps.action: Compare the model with slip-rate, strain-rate, style and direction observations through misfit maps; the fits are good except at the southern Hikurangi margin and in local areas.
steps.quote: The method described above produces a kinematic model that fits observations (Figures 5 and 6)

steps.action: Report the inferred slip rates and uncertainties for the Hikurangi margin (45 ± 8, 34 ± 3, 20 ± 3 mm/yr shortening), the Wellington-Marlborough faults, the Alpine Fault and the Puysegur faults.
steps.quote: we model a total of 45 ± 8 mm/yr of shortening in northern Hikurangi and 34 ± 3 mm/yr in central Hikurangi

steps.action: Compare HS22-Lit with the eta = 1e-7 per year model, which does not overfit; velocity differences are small, but the partition between on-fault and off-fault deformation changes.
steps.quote: which does not overfit observations, are generally small compared to the uncertainty in the models.

steps.action: Compare the long-term velocity field with the contemporary GPS velocity field (Beavan et al. 2016; Haines & Wallace 2020) and interpret the differences as interseismic locking on the Alpine Fault and the southern Hikurangi thrust.
steps.quote: displays some notable differences from the contemporary velocity field determined from GPS observations

steps.action: State two rival explanations for the smaller long-term rotation of northeastern North Island: a transient geodetic signal, or an inaccurate long-term velocity field.
steps.quote: Two possibilities arise for why our predicted rotation of northeastern North Island is

steps.action: Reject the transient-signal explanation by argument, because a dextral transient signal is unlikely to be consistent with subduction locking; attribute the mismatch to missing dextral slip or to Havre Trough parameters.
Compare the Hikurangi shortening rates with the Wallace et al. (2004) estimates: smaller values but the same southward-decreasing pattern.
steps.quote: this is smaller than the respective values of 54 ± 6 mm/yr and 44 ± 7 mm/yr modeled by Wallace et al. (2004)

steps.action: Identify large misfits at the Alpine-Kelly-Hope intersection, showing that the input slip rates are mutually incompatible, and infer about 9 mm/yr of motion as distributed strain southeast of the Alpine Fault.
steps.quote: This indicates that the estimated fault slip rates in this region are inconsistent with each other

steps.action: Repeat the modeling with the NZ Community Fault Model v1.0 in place of Litchfield et al. (2014) (HS22-CFM); velocity differences are typically below 5 mm/yr and the Hikurangi rates are mostly consistent.
steps.quote: We repeat our modeling using the recently released New Zealand Community Fault Model (NZ CFM) v1.0

steps.action: Check that HS22-CFM, given the fast Holocene Akatore rate, returns a slow rate consistent with the independent long-term rate of Taylor-Silva et al. (2020).
steps.quote: HS22-CFM models a significantly smaller horizontal slip rate of 0.05 mm/yr

steps.action: Keep the model's slip-rate estimates, including Hikurangi shortening rates smaller than earlier estimates, and flag regions of missing or incompatible slip.
steps.quote: Our HS22-Lit model predicts shortening rates across the Hikurangi subduction margin that are significantly smaller than previously published estimates.

tree.answer: Quaternary long-term deformation across the NZ plate boundary, on faults and between them
Partly: slip rates on mapped faults are observed; off-fault strain and subduction rates are latent
Estimate a kinematic velocity field and fault slip rates with uncertainties
No rivals for the main estimate; two rival explanations for the NE North Island GPS mismatch
Not computed; the rivals are weighed by argument
Found: compiled geological slip rates and known plate motions
Velocities are robust to eta and to the choice of fault database; the on-fault/off-fault partition is sensitive
Estimates kept with Monte Carlo uncertainties

end.claim: Balancing the plate-motion budget gives Hikurangi margin shortening of 45 ± 8, 34 ± 3 and 20 ± 3 mm/yr (north, central, south), lower and better constrained than previous estimates, together with improved slip rates and uncertainties on all modeled faults.

decisive_move.sentence: The plate-motion-constrained iterative thin-sheet regression with Monte Carlo uncertainties turns compiled fault slip rates into budget-consistent slip-rate estimates; without it there are no subduction rate estimates.

gates.evidence: The data are compiled from Litchfield et al. (2014); no hypothesis directed their acquisition. The model faced misfit checks (Figures 5-6), a rerun with an alternative database, and the Akatore check, which could have failed, but there is no crucial test of the Hikurangi estimates. Eta was chosen after fitting as the best fit (p. 11), and the uncertainty inflation was set by judgment (pp. 6-7).

imports.item: Monte Carlo resampling of observations to estimate uncertainties and covariances
Central Limit behavior used to argue that output uncertainties are Gaussian
Newtonian viscous rheology and work-rate minimization (thin viscous sheet)

novelty_claims.quote: these rates are lower and better constrained by regional kinematics than previous estimates
We make new statistically robust estimates of slip rates and uncertainties on all faults, including the Hikurangi subduction zone
Unlike previous models, we include discontinuities at faults in the model, allowing us to improve the resolution of the model from ∼100 km to <10 [...]

limits:
No review file was supplied; the acknowledgments mention an Associate Editor and two reviewers, but their requests are unknown. The paper does not show how many eta values or parameter settings were tried before the reported sweep, nor whether the uncertainty inflation factors (four times, half, factor five) were tuned against the outcome (inference: they were set by judgment, given as reasonable). The Monte Carlo varies only fault slip-rate observations, not boundary velocities, style observations or uncertainty choices (inference from p. 11). The robustness rerun with NZ CFM is not independent, since the CFM draws heavily on Litchfield. The GPS comparison is not a test of the long-term field, because differences are expected from locking.

Sub-claims and their statuses: about 9 mm/yr of unaccounted motion in central South Island (estimate_with_resolution); the Alpine-Kelly-Hope slip rates are mutually incompatible (estimate_with_resolution, a misfit finding); missing dextral slip of 5-10 mm/yr in NE North Island (best_explanation, a rival rejected by argument only, testing deferred to fieldwork); strong coupling of the southern Hikurangi thrust (best_explanation, consistent with cited work); fault slip rates over-estimated in Wellington-Marlborough (stated in the Plain Language Summary, weakly supported in the text).

Composition is none_fits: the walk is a regularized estimation from compiled trace data with robustness checks, with no rivals for the main claim, no natural repetition fitted, and no new capability as the core.

disagreements.target: Wallace et al. (2004) Hikurangi shortening rates
disagreements.support: The budget-constrained model gives 45 ± 8 and 34 ± 3 mm/yr against 54 ± 6 and 44 ± 7 mm/yr, with the same southward-decreasing pattern.
disagreements.quote: this is smaller than the respective values of 54 ± 6 mm/yr and 44 ± 7 mm/yr modeled by Wallace et al. (2004)

disagreements.target: Litchfield et al. (2014) slip rates at the Alpine-Kelly-Hope intersection
disagreements.support: Under strain compatibility the model cannot fit the input rates; it gives 18 ± 4 mm/yr on the Kelly Fault against 13 ± 2 mm/yr.
disagreements.quote: This indicates that the estimated fault slip rates in this region are inconsistent with each other

disagreements.target: Current fault slip-rate models of central South Island (Litchfield et al., 2014)
disagreements.support: The model needs about 9 mm/yr of distributed motion southeast of the Alpine Fault that no known fault rate accounts for.
disagreements.quote: there is ∼9 mm/yr of plate motion in central South Island not accounted for by current models of fault slip rates

disagreements.target: NZ CFM v1.0 Holocene Akatore Fault slip rate
disagreements.support: Given the 0.9 mm/yr Holocene input, HS22-CFM returns 0.05 mm/yr, consistent with the long-term rate.
disagreements.quote: kinematic and strain compatibility constraints likely require the Akatore Fault to average the slower rate over longer timescales

disagreements.support: Its sparse 32-vertex mesh treats many faults collectively, so it misses detailed deformation features.
disagreements.quote: Lamb's model is calculated from a sparse mesh that treats many faults collectively rather than separately.

disagreements.target: Elastic block models combining GPS and geology (Wallace et al., 2004, 2007, 2012)
disagreements.support: The paper argues that geodetic and geological timescales differ and that block geometry limits conclusions.
disagreements.quote: These models assume that contemporary and geological deformation are comparable, and conclusions are limited by the assumed geometry of blocks.

disagreements.support: Continuum models ignore velocity discontinuities at faults; block models ignore deformation between faults.
disagreements.quote: they do not account for deformation occurring between faults and, therefore, underestimate deformation.

disagreements.target: Existing fault slip-rate estimates in the Wellington-Marlborough region
disagreements.support: Based on the comparison of the long-term model with GPS; the main text gives little detail.
disagreements.quote: fault slip rates are over-estimated in the Wellington– Marlborough region (lowering hazard there).
